standfirst: A psychology professor loses her son, the courts shrug, she settles it herself inside the first hour, and the remaining thirteen episodes are about what that costs her. No twist, no clever structure, no slow build. Kim Nam Joo is extraordinary and Cha Eun Woo has never been better used. The plot is not new and the performances make it land anyway. Below: revenge and grief handled with the same seriousness.

picks.why: A woman who has already decided, working the plan. Same architecture as Wonderful World: the decision happens early, and the drama is in the execution and the collateral. Both are anchored by an actress who can hold a scene without raising her voice. Difference: The Glory is intricate and patient, built on years of preparation, where Wonderful World does the deed in episode one and then lives with it.

Women against an institution that owns the outcome in advance. Shares the specific fury of Wonderful World: the legal system is not broken, it is functioning exactly as designed for the people who paid for it. Kim Go Eun and a plot that keeps escalating. Difference: it is a stylised thriller with money at the centre, and the last stretch goes so far off the rails that the ending divides.

Grief that has curdled into obsession, in a town that wants it forgotten. Both are about a parent or a survivor who will not let a death be filed away, and both are more interested in the damage that does to the person than in the case. Career-best work from Shin Ha Kyun. Difference: it is a slow procedural with a genuine mystery, and it withholds everything for ten hours.

A mother whose whole self has been spent on a child. The same maternal engine as Wonderful World, comedy on top and a legal injustice underneath, and both are unusually honest that the loss reorganises the parent permanently. Difference: it is a village comedy for long stretches and its violence stays offscreen.

A woman rebuilding what actually happened to her family. Same MBC melodrama register: an articulate professional woman, a death that has been mislabelled, and an investigation she is not qualified to run. Kim Ha Neul is very good in it. Difference: it is a marriage thriller first, so the antagonist is domestic rather than institutional.

What the courts do with a child who kills. Wonderful World starts from a sentence that satisfied nobody, and this is ten episodes inside that machinery, with a judge who despises the people running it. The complement rather than the echo. Difference: it is procedural, unemotional by design, and it gives you no revenge at all.

against.title: The World of the Married
against.why: Paired for the MBC-grade intensity and the wronged woman at the centre. It is about a marriage, and every escalation is about possession and humiliation between spouses. Wonderful World is about a dead child and a legal system, which is a different pain entirely.

against.title: Mine
against.why: Paired for the wealthy-family-under-pressure angle. It is a stylish chaebol drama about women taking control of a house, and its stakes are inheritance and reputation. Nothing in it is about grief.

against.title: Mother
against.why: The other Korean drama that gets named for a woman who takes the law into her own hands for a child. It is a quieter, sadder, better-reviewed piece about protecting a living child rather than avenging a dead one. Fine viewing later, wrong appetite now.
